title: Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020
short_title: Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would overhaul how Australia pays for higher education and make universities more accountable for student results.
It would amend the Higher Education Support Act to tie funding to graduate job outcomes and to give regional and Indigenous Australians more places.
The explanatory memorandum does not specify the dollar amounts or the exact start date of the changes.
changes: Encourage universities to produce graduates with skills the job market needs.
Expand study opportunities for people in rural and remote areas, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.
Toughen student protection and require universities to be more answerable for what their students achieve.
summary.affected: Higher education providers, students, and taxpayers.

The amendments will reintroduce a [10% discount](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fems%2Fr6584_ems_83be00d4-bab9-48e1-9590-3ab27d90e7eb%22;rec=0) on up-front payments made by HECS-HELP students and the [Student Learning Entitlement](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fems%2Fr6584_ems_83be00d4-bab9-48e1-9590-3ab27d90e7eb%22;rec=0) (SLE). ### What does the bill do? This bill will implement part of the government's [Job Ready Graduates Package](https://www.dese.gov.au/job-ready) and includes major proposed higher education funding changes, including how the government currently subsidises university tuition costs. If successful in its current form, the bill will decrease the subsidy for most areas of the humanities and social science as well as in engineering, science, surveying, environmental studies and other areas. On the other hand, it will increase the subsidy for most health fields, education, mathematics and other areas. At the same time, the bill will set new maximum student contribution amounts, which means the degree costs for students are going to change significantly. Humanities, law and commerce degrees are going to increase in price while mathematics, agriculture and certain science degrees will decrease. Sometimes, such as in the case of engineering, the changes appear somewhat contradictory: both the subsidy for engineering and the maximum student contribution rate is being reduced. speeches.speaker: Dan Tehan
speeches.brief: The bill creates 39,000 additional university places by 2023 and 100,000 over ten years, with cheaper degrees in teaching, nursing, and other areas of expected job demand, including a 42% reduction for teaching and languages, 59% for agriculture and maths, and 18% for science and IT. It also establishes a $900 million National Priorities and Industry Linkage Fund, implements Napthine review recommendations on regional and Indigenous student support, and introduces grandfathering to protect current students.

speeches.speaker: Tanya Plibersek
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to reject the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it makes university harder and more expensive, with 40% of students facing fee increases up to $14,500 per year and some degrees more than doubling in cost. They claimed the bill cuts billions from universities, fails to address youth unemployment or demand for places, and would reduce funding for teaching engineering, science, and maths by 16–32%, contrary to the government’s stated aims.

speeches.speaker: Patrick Gorman
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020 is a tax on students that increases fees—humanities by 113%, law and commerce by 28%, and 40% of students facing fees of $14,500 a year—while cutting university funding, with UWA losing 3–4% revenue, Curtin University $60 million, and 21,000 staff jobs at risk.

speeches.speaker: Helen Haines
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020 because it implements key Napthine review recommendations, including $160 million in tertiary access payments, guaranteed Commonwealth places for Indigenous regional students, and increased funding for regional universities, but called for the Senate to refer the bill to the Education and Employment Legislation Committee for review due to concerns over rushed, evidence‑poor changes to student fees that disproportionately affect regional students.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it would increase humanities fees by up to 113%, making university unaffordable for low- and middle-income families, disproportionately affecting women and Indigenous Australians, and representing government interference in students' career choices. He called for the bill to go to a Senate inquiry.

speeches.speaker: Elizabeth Coker
speeches.brief: Labor opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it would increase student fees, cut Commonwealth funding, shift debt to students, and harm universities, particularly affecting young people in Corangamite and Victoria during COVID-19.

speeches.speaker: Zali Steggall
speeches.brief: The bill was opposed for redirecting university funding toward STEM at the expense of humanities, arts, commerce and law, and for including a punitive 50 per cent completion rule that removes loan eligibility; the government was urged to delay implementation by at least two years, grandfather existing students' fees, extend the Indigenous eligibility definition to all Indigenous persons, and refer the bill to the Senate Education and Employment Legislation Committee. Specific concerns included a $4,758 per-student shortfall for science degrees, a rise in student contribution share from 42 to 52 per cent, and a predicted 30 per cent increase in suicides among 15- to 24-year-olds over five years due to COVID-19.

speeches.speaker: Peter Khalil
speeches.brief: The bill makes it harder and more expensive for young Australians to go to university, with 40% of students facing fee increases of up to 113%—including humanities degrees rising from $27,216 to $58,000—while cutting guaranteed university funding by around a billion dollars a year, and the speaker argued this will limit access to humanities education for disadvantaged students and undermine critical thinking skills needed for future jobs.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The bill was opposed for increasing student fees and cutting university funding, with regional students and universities disproportionately affected. Specific criticisms included a $1 billion annual funding cut, a 7% average fee increase, humanities degree fees rising from $27,216 to $58,000, and the exclusion of universities from JobKeeper.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it would double the cost of many degrees, increase the student share of university funding from 42% to 48%, and deter young people from higher education, while advocating for free education funded by taxing billionaires and corporations.

speeches.speaker: Susan Templeman
speeches.brief: The Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020 was opposed for increasing student fees—with 40% of students facing $14,500 per year—reducing university funding for STEM courses, and disproportionately harming disadvantaged students and those from Western Sydney, while the government provided no additional university places or JobKeeper for university staff.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it cuts $1 billion from universities, raises student fees by up to 113% for humanities, and removes loadings from enabling programs at the University of Newcastle despite its regional campuses in Taree, Moree, Orange, Port Macquarie and Coffs Harbour. They criticised the Morrison government for excluding universities from JobKeeper and warned that 21,000 university jobs face elimination within six months.

speeches.speaker: David Smith
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment bill, arguing it would cut university funding by around $1 billion per year, increase student fees by an average of 7% (with humanities fees doubling to $58,000), and harm regional universities, women, and First Nations students, citing cuts to per-student funding for engineering (16%), nursing (8%), and teaching (6%).

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Amendment (Job-Ready Graduates and Supporting Regional and Remote Students) Bill 2020, arguing it entrenches privilege rather than allowing access based on merit, and criticised cuts of $3 billion from TAFE and a reduction of 140,000 apprentices and trainees under the government.
